AZ-2026-HB2016.s: This law changes Arizona tax penalty rules for late or missing returns and other tax filing problems. It affects taxpayers and some businesses that file or pay state taxes, including people who miss deadlines, give wrong information, or fail to pay amounts owed. The law also sets or changes penalty amounts for some tobacco tax and cigarette label violations.

AZ-2026-HB2100.s: Counties would be allowed to set rules for small land subdivisions of 6 to 10 lots on land that is not subject to certain water supply rules, as long as each lot is at least 2 acres. A person applying for one would need to file a public report and make sure each lot has legal access. If a county adopts such a rule, it would have to give written notice to the state real estate department. The bill passed the legislature but was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2105.s: The measure would require the state tax department and county assessors to tell property owners before an on-site inspection and give the inspection date. They would also have to give the owner a copy of the inspection report, and the notice would not have to be sent by certified mail. For farm property, it keeps the yearly inspection and four-year appraisal rules, and blocks another on-site inspection for three years after the last one unless there is a change in use, a split, a change in ownership or lease, or a taxable improvement.

AZ-2026-HB2114.s: The law changes motorcycle registration rules and sets up a motorcycle safety fund. A motorcycle registration can be renewed only if at least one owner is licensed to ride in Arizona, with a 30-day temporary registration allowed for someone enrolled in approved training. The state must put $1 from each motorcycle registration fee into the fund, which can pay for motorcycle safety programs and some training scholarships. It was signed into law on June 22, 2026, and takes effect after December 31, 2026.

AZ-2026-HB2133.s: The bill would require commercial websites that publish sexual material to verify that each depicted person gave written, verifiable consent and was at least 18 when the material was made. It would also require them to keep verification records for seven years and use reasonable steps to block uploads without verified consent. The bill would expand rules on unlawful disclosure of nude or sexual images to include synthetic depictions made with artificial intelligence or other technology, and it would let the state and the person shown bring civil cases.

AZ-2026-HB2140.s: The bill would let the state treasurer invest some trust and treasury money in physical gold or silver bullion, up to 10% of the total value, if it is kept in a U.S. precious metals depository that meets storage, insurance, audit, and separate-holding rules. It would also update other rules on how the treasurer can invest state money and lend securities. The measure passed the legislature but was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2170.s: The bill would bar some China-based companies from bidding on or getting Arizona state contracts for electronic or information technology. Companies that seek these contracts would have to sign a letter saying they are not covered by the ban and are not buying from a banned company for resale. A false letter could bring a $100,000 fine, contract ending, and a 60-month ban on bidding for state contracts.

AZ-2026-HB2174.s: This law updates Arizona insurance rules by replacing the term "advisory organization" with "modeling and data organization" in several places. It lets these groups gather and share insurance data and lets the insurance director review and examine them under the same kinds of rules. It also keeps the current rules for rate making, data sharing, and penalties for late reports.

AZ-2026-HB2226.s: The law requires a court to ask a person at their first court appearance whether they are a veteran. If the court confirms veteran status, it must notify the prosecutor, and the person may be told about services from the state veterans agency and may be considered for veterans court or another treatment or diversion program in some cases. If veteran status is unclear, the prosecutor must let the person or their lawyer show proof, such as a DD-214 form, which is a discharge record from the military.

AZ-2026-HB2257.s: This law changes how money from watercraft registration and infrastructure fees is split among the watercraft licensing fund, the state lake improvement fund, and the law enforcement and boating safety fund. It also sends certain additional registration fees to a multi-county water conservation district account for the lower Colorado river multispecies conservation program and requires the department to file an annual report on spending from the watercraft licensing fund.

AZ-2026-HB2265.s: Arizona changed several court fee rules and fee limits for criminal and civil cases. It bars courts from charging many fees or reimbursements to indigent people, juveniles, and criminal defendants for public defense, appeals, and some transcripts, while also changing how some court fees and jury fees are collected and used. The law was signed by the governor on June 19, 2026.

AZ-2026-HB2305.s: The bill would make private towing rates for cars from private property a state matter, so counties, cities, and towns could not add more local rules on those rates. In places that had not set rates by January 1, 2026, the towing, storage, and impound rate would follow the Department of Public Safety tow service agreement for that area, and local governments that already set rates would have to update them by July 1, 2027. It would also set rules for tow signs, photos, police notice, vehicle release, receipts, and penalties for private towing carriers and some property owners.

AZ-2026-HB2321.s: The law requires the Department of Child Safety to place a credit freeze on a child’s credit record within 30 days after the child is found dependent and placed in the department’s care. The freeze stays in place until the child turns 16, when the child can choose to keep it or remove it, and the department must notify the parent or guardian when the freeze is placed or remains in place. It also updates state rules for credit reporting agencies on how to place or remove these freezes, and says they may not charge a fee for doing so.

AZ-2026-HB2322.s: The bill would require the Department of Child Safety to record, by audio or video, interviews it conducts with children, unless equipment fails or is not available. It would also require the department to apply for federal grants for that recording work if such grants are created, and the law would take effect only if that federal grant law is enacted by December 31, 2036. The bill passed the Legislature but was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2327.s: The law lets certain people ask a court to keep their identifying information out of county recorder records. It applies to many public safety workers, public officials, judges, some state workers, and people in certain safety programs or protection orders. If a judge approves the request, the county recorder must restrict access for five years, and the law also sets rules for filing, notice, and later removal of those limits.

AZ-2026-HB2379.s: The bill would require school district governing board members to complete an 8-hour training on school finance and related board duties. County school superintendents or the state education department would provide the training, and school districts could be charged for the cost. It would also add reporting rules and could make some board members in high-risk districts ineligible to run or be appointed again if they do not meet the training rules.

AZ-2026-HB2380.s: School district governing boards would have to meet at the most convenient public place in the district when one is available, and could meet elsewhere if no such place is available. They could also approve salary or other expense orders between meetings if the board had already passed a resolution and later ratified the order. The bill also changes some school board powers tied to district money and other duties.

AZ-2026-HB2406.s: The law changes rules for county medical examiners and for records that show deceased minors. It makes autopsy photos, videos, and digital images of a deceased minor confidential, and limits who can get them. It also adds stronger privacy rules for crime victims’ records and images, including limits on release to the public.

AZ-2026-HB2408.s: The measure would update Arizona nursing law, including the rules the state nursing board uses for terms like license, certification, and disciplinary action. It would affect nurses and other people regulated by the board. The bill also deals with regulatory actions and expungement, which means removing or sealing certain records.

AZ-2026-HB2482.s: The bill would change rules for Arizona school building renewal grants and how school districts apply for them. It would add more reporting, inspection, and project review steps, and it would set a $1,000,000 cap on an individual job order for construction work paid with building renewal grant money. It would affect school districts and the state offices that manage school facility funding, but it was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2592.s: The bill would set rules for Arizona state agencies and other budget units on how they use artificial intelligence. It would require them to look for ways to use AI to cut admin work, lower costs, improve service, and use existing staff and resources, and it would limit new AI-specific rules unless the legislature clearly allows them. It would also require emergency or temporary AI rules to be ratified by the legislature. The bill was passed by both chambers but was later vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2661.s: The law updates the rights notice that child safety workers must give to parents, guardians, and custodians during abuse or neglect investigations. It adds a notice that a parent or guardian may delegate temporary guardianship of a child. It also keeps the rule that the department must explain these rights in person and in writing and get a written acknowledgment of receipt.

AZ-2026-HB2700.s: Arizona would create a temporary study committee on assistive technology. The group would meet twice a year, study new tools and ways to better serve people who use assistive technology, and submit a report by October 1, 2027. Some members could be paid back for travel and other allowed expenses, and the committee would end on that same date.

AZ-2026-HB2729.s: This law continues the Arizona state board of nursing through July 1, 2030, and sets it to end on January 1, 2031. It also continues several other state boards and the Department of Economic Security on the same schedule, or in the case of the pharmacy board, through July 1, 2032. The changes apply from and after July 1, 2026.

AZ-2026-HB2762.s: Signed into law, this act requires foods made from cultivated cells to have a label on the package saying "cell-cultivated" or "cell-cultured." It applies to the manufacturer, packager, or retailer of those foods. The law was approved by the governor on June 19, 2026.

AZ-2026-HB2782.s: The bill requires the Arizona Corporation Commission and public utilities to disclose how costs tied to regulatory assets are recovered in rates, including the amortization schedule. It also says tariff schedules that affect rates should be posted publicly so people can review and comment on them. The bill was passed and signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2793.s: The bill would change the rules for how cities and towns in Arizona annex, or add, nearby land. It sets steps for filing, notices, hearings, petitions, and public review, and it lets a city or town skip the waiting period and hearing if one property owner controls all the land to be annexed. It also changes some map, notice, and zoning rules for annexed land and was passed and signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2830.s: The bill would have required Arizona schools to teach fetal and prenatal human development in science classes, with the state board setting the grade levels and standards. It would have required lessons on stages of development, major milestones, and support structures like the placenta and umbilical cord. Schools would not have been allowed to include sex education topics in this instruction, and parents would not have had opt-out rights for it under the bill's rules. It was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-HB2957.s: It would change state rules on driver licenses, including mobile and enhanced versions, and would affect drivers and the state transportation department.

AZ-2026-HB2960.s: This law creates a grant program for cities and counties to start or grow veterans' court programs, and it creates a veterans' treatment court fund to pay for them. The fund can help cover program costs, including staff, and the state court office will run the program, set rules, and collect yearly reports on results. It became law on June 22, 2026.

AZ-2026-HB2970.s: The bill would update Arizona’s fraud law to say the state can prosecute a case if one part of the scheme happened in Arizona or within one local area here, even if other parts happened elsewhere. It would also say that a fraud scheme includes taking away a person’s right to honest services. The change would affect people charged with fraudulent schemes and artifices.

AZ-2026-HB2979.s: The bill changes Arizona rules for credit unions. It sets time limits for the state deputy director to respond to requests about bylaw changes, name changes, and changes to a main office or branch, and it lets credit unions ask to use powers tied to out-of-state credit unions by filing a request. It also updates rules on credit committee votes, share accounts, and several other credit union powers.

AZ-2026-HB2995.s: This law changes how courts handle child custody and parenting time when domestic violence is involved. It says domestic violence must be treated as against the child’s best interests, and it creates a strong presumption against giving legal decision-making or parenting time to a parent who committed it. Courts must look at more kinds of evidence and make detailed findings on the record when they decide these cases.

AZ-2026-HB4010.s: Arizona would create a Board of Genetic Counselors to license and regulate genetic counselors. It requires people to be licensed to work as genetic counselors in the state, with some exceptions for other licensed health workers and federal workers. The board would keep an online list of licensed genetic counselors and set rules for licensing, fees, and discipline.

AZ-2026-HB4043.s: Beginning August 1, 2026, public high schools that sponsor sports would have to provide an automated external defibrillator, or AED, at each campus and at school sports events, and keep it in a marked, easy-to-reach place. Beginning August 1, 2027, each school district and charter school would have to have at least one staff member at each campus during regular hours trained in CPR and first aid, and also trained to use an AED if one is on campus. Schools could accept gifts and donations to help buy and maintain AEDs. The bill was signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1012.s: The measure would remove two rules tied to concealed handguns at restaurants that serve liquor. It would end language saying a concealed handgun alone does not require a restaurant licensee or employee to step in or call police, and it would also end a special exception for restaurant licensees when a serious act of violence is caused by a concealed handgun. The bill passed but was later vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1013.s: The bill would have barred the state and local governments from using hiring rules that require jobs to be filled on anything other than merit, meaning a person's skills, experience, and ability. It would also have limited efforts to shape the makeup of employees by race, ethnicity, sex, or national origin, except as needed to follow anti-discrimination laws. It would have allowed lawsuits for violations and was passed before being vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1037.s: The measure would change voter registration checks, including when county recorders mail notices, mark a voter inactive, or cancel a registration after an address change. It would also require the secretary of state to keep Arizona in a multistate electronic voter registration system, and it would change rules for presidential preference election ballots and early voting. It would affect county recorders, election officials, and registered voters. The bill passed the Legislature but was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1040.s: The bill would require county recorders to make voter registration rolls available to the public through an internet portal that lets people download the information. It would bar fees for that access or for the information itself. The bill also says voter registration records and related lists may be used only for election, political, or other legally allowed purposes.

AZ-2026-SB1046.s: The bill would bar Arizona telecommunications infrastructure from using equipment made by China or other foreign-adversary companies, and would require providers to remove and replace banned equipment. It would also require providers to certify each year to the Corporation Commission that they are not using banned equipment, and it sets civil penalties of at least $10,000 per day and up to $100,000 per day for violations. Providers that do not comply could also be blocked from receiving certain state, local, and federal money for telecommunications infrastructure. If enacted, it would take effect after December 31, 2026.

AZ-2026-SB1094.s: The bill would create a paid family and medical leave insurance program in Arizona. Starting in 2028, employers and employees would pay payroll contributions to fund it, and starting in 2029 eligible workers could get paid leave for a new child, a serious health condition, pregnancy or childbirth, military leave needs, or safe leave for domestic or sexual violence. It would also protect a worker's job when the leave ends and set benefit limits and payment rules.

AZ-2026-SB1113.s: This law changes who may serve certain court papers in cases for involuntary evaluation or court-ordered treatment. It lets the court authorize a person employed by a screening agency or evaluation agency to serve the papers if the proposed patient is already at that facility when the petition is filed. It also says an evaluation agency or screening agency is not financially responsible for serving those documents.

AZ-2026-SB1124.s: The bill would require a health profession board to give a health professional at least 14 days’ notice before voting on a psychological or psychiatric evaluation, along with a summary of the complaint or issue that led to the review. It would let the professional send a written reply and speak at a hearing, and the board would have to consider that reply. If the board ordered the evaluation, it would have to give the professional a copy of it, and if no action came from the evaluation, the board would have to pay back the cost. The bill passed the legislature but was vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1133.s: The bill would let a candidate for state or local office use a financial disclosure form already filed for that year as a public officer, so no extra filing would be needed for that year. It affects people filing nomination papers for office in Arizona. It was passed and signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1160.s: The law limits drone use near ticketed entertainment events like concerts, sports, and shows held in gated areas. It makes it a crime to fly a drone within 5,280 feet of or above such an event unless the flyer has permission or fits a listed exception, like certain workers or flying over their own property for noncommercial use. It also keeps cities and counties from making their own rules on drone ownership or use in most cases.

AZ-2026-SB1165.s: The bill makes some health plans stop charging copays, deductibles, and other out-of-pocket costs for certain breast exams. It applies to hospital service corporations, health care service organizations, and disability insurers for policies or contracts issued, changed, delivered, or renewed on or after January 1, 2027. For high-deductible plans, the no-cost rule generally starts after the deductible is met, with an exception for preventive care.

AZ-2026-SB1189.s: The law changes rules for revitalization districts, which are public groups that handle local projects and services. It lets them make more contracts, set user fees, borrow money, and work with towns, tribes, and others on infrastructure, but it bars them from using district money for pro sports stadiums or team-only facilities. It also requires new construction contracts to include rules that let contractors and subcontractors stop work if they are not paid, and it applies to contracts signed after the law takes effect.

AZ-2026-SB1198.s: The bill continues the Arizona Beef Council, a self-funded program that helps market and grow beef sales in Arizona and beyond. It sets the council to end on July 1, 2034, with repeal of related law on January 1, 2035. The change applies back to July 1, 2026, and the bill was signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1205.s: The law limits what cities and towns can do about wheel boots on private property and sets state rules for when booting is allowed. It requires signs at private lots, sets release rules, and says booting services must be able to release a vehicle 24 hours a day. It also sets booting fees at $90 to $150, allows some added fees in limited cases, and bars booting certain vehicles like marked emergency vehicles, tax-exempt plate vehicles, and cars with an occupant.

AZ-2026-SB1206.s: The law changes rules for storm-related insurance claims and for contractors who do post-storm home repair or replacement work. It limits when contractors can start work, requires written disclosures and cancellation rights, and bars contractors from promising to cover deductibles or acting as an adjuster for the insured on the claim. It also sets rules for adjusters, including limits on working on damaged property and on some actions during an active emergency response.

AZ-2026-SB1215.s: The bill expands Arizona’s workers’ compensation cancer presumption for firefighters, fire investigators, and certain peace officers. It adds more kinds of cancer to the list that are treated as work-related if the worker meets set job and exam rules, such as years on hazardous duty and a clear pre-employment exam. It also lets some former firefighters, fire investigators, and peace officers use this presumption for up to 15 years after their last job date if they are 65 or younger.

AZ-2026-SB1221.s: The bill would limit when the tax department can apply a new reading of tax law to taxpayers, and it would block retroactive tax, penalty, or interest charges in those cases. It would also require notice to the Senate Finance and House Ways & Means committees before a new reading is adopted, and it would allow a hearing on its effect on taxpayers. The measure would also set rules for refunds tied to past tax amounts and define "new interpretation or application" to include rules, tax rulings, procedures, and return instructions.

AZ-2026-SB1242.s: Arizona’s mental health law was changed to allow hearings and evaluations to use audiovisual technology, such as remote video, in some cases. The changes apply to mental health services, courts, and health care workers who handle these cases. The bill passed and was signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1246.s: Arizona would raise the bar for a homeowners' association to foreclose on a condo unit for unpaid common charges. It would require the owner to be delinquent for 18 months or owe at least $10,000, and for special charges of $10,000 or more, only the 18-month rule would apply. The bill also says the board should try to contact the owner and offer a payment plan before filing foreclosure. It also changes how some unit owner charges are treated and how payments are applied.

AZ-2026-SB1270.s: The bill lets some correctional officers in the state retirement plan get an extra employer payment into their retirement account. The extra payment can be up to $5,000 per worker, can be given at set service milestones, and does not require the worker to add more money. It also says these payments are optional for employers and can be stopped later.

AZ-2026-SB1274.s: Creates a special license plate for a police foundation in Arizona.

AZ-2026-SB1286.s: The bill lets a veterinarian form a client-patient relationship through electronic means, except for animals used in commercial food production. It requires client consent, gives clients the vet’s contact and license info, and says the vet must explain limits on care by video or other electronic visits. It also lets vets prescribe drugs after an electronic exam, with limits on renewals and no controlled substances unless the vet has done an in-person exam or timely on-site visits. The bill passed and was signed by the Governor.

AZ-2026-SB1336.s: This law changes how the state land department handles state trust land, including rules for public records, appraisals, maps, and lease or permit timing. It also sets new duties for the department to make and update military-related maps and share them with the public, counties, cities, and the state real estate department. The law also changes how conceptual land use plans are made for state trust land and when they are updated.

AZ-2026-SB1345.s: The law creates a legislative task force on perimenopause and menopause. The group must study care, education, and how providers might be paid for this care, and it must send reports by December 31, 2027 and December 31, 2028. Members serve without pay, can get expense refunds, and the task force ends on June 30, 2029.

AZ-2026-SB1399.s: The bill appropriates $160 million from the state general fund in fiscal year 2026-2027 to the Department of Economic Security for child care assistance. It also says this money will not lapse, meaning it can stay available instead of expiring at the end of the year. The bill was signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1416.s: The law changes how police must report missing or kidnapped children. It requires quicker sharing of child details with state and national missing-child systems, notice to the national missing and exploited children center, and training for officers who handle these cases. It also keeps child records in the system until the child is found or the case is closed.

AZ-2026-SB1419.s: The law changes rules for solar energy devices and other small power systems in Arizona. It updates contract and disclosure rules for sales and leases, and says installers must meet licensing, training, and safety rules. It also adds roof checks for contractors before putting solar devices on a roof and affects sellers, buyers, lessors, and installers of these systems.

AZ-2026-SB1428.s: Arizona law would add new rules for workers' compensation policies with zero estimated exposure, meaning a policy for an employer that reports no payroll exposure. It would require the applicant to sign a statement saying the information is true and that they have no employees, and if they hire someone during the policy period, they must tell the insurer within 60 days. For some construction businesses, it would also require giving contract partners a copy of the policy and notice, and certain insurance certificates would need a web link to check the policy. These rules would apply to policies and related insurance certificates made on or after July 1, 2027.

AZ-2026-SB1446.s: The law limits how often the state can require social workers at outpatient treatment centers that provide dialysis to record a patient’s progress in the medical record. It says that can be required no more than once every three months unless federal Medicare and Medicaid rules require more. It affects social workers and dialysis centers in Arizona.

AZ-2026-SB1452.s: Arizona would require the attorney general to set up a cargo theft task force to fight theft, fraud, and other crimes tied to cargo and freight. The task force would include law enforcement staff and would investigate cases, work with other agencies and industry partners, and suggest cases for prosecution. Starting July 1, 2027, the attorney general would send a yearly report on the task force's work and cargo theft trends.

AZ-2026-SB1456.s: The bill would change the rules for authorized third-party driver license providers in Arizona. It would require these providers to meet set bond, experience, space, and staff rules, and to follow department quality checks. It would also let them do some commercial driver license work if the director allows it and federal law permits.

AZ-2026-SB1493.s: The measure changes how some law enforcement discipline appeals work in superior court. It lets certain officers and local agencies seek court review after a hearing, and it allows some winning officers to get back pay and, in some cases, lawyer fees up to set limits. It was signed by the Governor.

AZ-2026-SB1497.s: This law changes rules for school district self-insurance programs, which are district plans that pay some losses themselves instead of buying full insurance. It lets districts form or join pooled programs, sets rules for trust funds, audits, and liability coverage, and requires some districts to get price quotes every three years. It also requires detailed cost, claim, drug, and enrollment data from the people who support these plans.

AZ-2026-SB1511.s: The bill would require a person with a nondomiciled commercial driver license to show lawful immigration status or lawful presence before driving a commercial motor vehicle in Arizona. If the driver cannot show proof, police could issue a citation, assess a civil penalty, and report the case to the licensing authority and federal trucking officials. It would also allow the driver to be placed out of service, require the motor carrier to get a replacement driver or move the truck within 24 hours, and could lead to impoundment of the truck and related cargo costs.

AZ-2026-SB1552.s: Arizona’s transportation agency law would update many word definitions in the vehicle code, including terms for driver licenses, electric bikes and scooters, autonomous vehicles, and other road and vehicle terms. The changes would affect drivers, vehicle owners, dealers, and people who use these kinds of vehicles. The bill passed and was signed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1560.s: Arizona raised the maximum loan from the water supply development revolving fund for water supply projects from $3 million to $20 million. The fund can also still be used for grants, technical help, debt purchases or refinancing, bond insurance help, running the fund, and water supply studies. The bill was signed into law on June 22, 2026.

AZ-2026-SB1563.s: The law continues Arizona’s barbering and cosmetology board and sets a new end date of July 1, 2034. It also changes some board fees, including lower amounts for several license and renewal fees, and sets new fees for eyelash technician registration to be set by the board. It adds new rules for barber licenses, including age, education, training, fees, and exam requirements, and says the law was signed by the governor on June 22, 2026.

AZ-2026-SB1573.s: The bill would bar courts from using religious sectarian law as a controlling or helpful source when making decisions. It would also add a new rule aimed at federal courts sitting in certain state-law cases and define what counts as religious sectarian law. The measure would also rename part of Arizona law on foreign laws and add new findings about state court power.

AZ-2026-SB1624.s: The bill would change how Arizona handles traffic tickets from photo radar and other photo enforcement systems. It would set a civil penalty of up to $75 for certain civil traffic violations from those systems, and it would say these violations cannot be used to suspend or revoke a driver license or to raise auto insurance rates. It would also keep drivers from having to identify who was in the photo or respond to a notice of violation, and it was later vetoed by the governor.

AZ-2026-SB1627.s: This law changes Arizona rules on drones and model aircraft. It makes it illegal to fly them in ways that break federal rules, interfere with emergency work, or intentionally fly over or near certain critical sites for a crime. It also bars local governments from making their own drone rules in most cases, with some exceptions for public agencies, first responders, and a few city park rules.

AZ-2026-SB1670.s: The bill would bar some landlords and rent-setting software companies from using algorithm-based tools that rely on private competitor data to help set rent, renewal terms, occupancy levels, or other lease terms for residential rentals. It would also let the Attorney General investigate and act on violations. The rule would apply to landlords with five or more rental units, mobile home spaces, or RV spaces, and to companies that sell or license these tools, with listed exceptions for certain housing and smaller landlords. The bill passed the Legislature but was vetoed by the Governor.

AZ-2026-SB1671.s: The law continues the state gaming department, the racing commission, and the boxing and mixed martial arts commission, and sets new end dates for them in 2032. It also requires leaders and employees in these agencies to file conflict-of-interest forms when hired or appointed and update them each year if anything changes. The gaming department must create a public complaint process and tracking system, file yearly complaint reports, and review older event wagering audits to check fee payments and fix any overpayments or underpayments.

AZ-2026-SB1683.s: The law limits foreign adversary nations and their agents from buying, leasing, or otherwise gaining a substantial interest in real property in Arizona. It also bars them from installing or operating certain equipment, like antennas, surveillance devices, or sensors, on property in the state. Beginning January 1, 2027, some utilities and government agencies must report suspected lease or equipment deals to the attorney general and the corporation commission. The law was signed by the governor and takes effect immediately.

AZ-2026-SB1713.s: Arizona would change how AHCCCS, the state health care program, chooses and reviews managed care contractors. It would set a new process that uses a published performance score, a four-year review period, and rules for who can get or keep contracts, starting October 1, 2026. The law also sets limits on enrollment levels for contractors and applies to AHCCCS, long-term care, and children’s health insurance programs.

AZ-2026-SB1723.s: The new law changes the rules for domestic violence protection orders. It lets a court require the defendant to give the other person identifying details, like a home address, job place, or vehicle info, if there is reason to think physical harm may happen. It also adds rules about notice if a person who was given exclusive use of the home moves out, and it keeps and serves these orders through the court and law enforcement.

AZ-2026-SB1808.s: The law changes rules for condominium and homeowners' associations on flag displays, political signs, and related group gatherings. It adds flags from nations allied with the United States to the list of flags an association may not ban from outdoor display, and it keeps limits on how associations can regulate size, placement, and timing. It also says associations may not stop unit owners from peacefully meeting in common areas to discuss condo issues, with some rules still allowed.
